Content:
Suppose we are given the graph of [MATH: y=f(x),] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/959569c0ed26a3e3cf9dca94c30a1bf8]

Content:
Given the graph of [MATH: y=f(x),] how can we use graph transformations to plot the graph of

Content:
[MATH: y=f\left(2x-4\right)+1 \, ?]

Content:
In this particular situation, we have to combine several operations.

Content:
To perform transformations of functions with multiple operations, we must apply the following rule:

Content:
1. First, we perform the transformations inside the argument of [MATH: f.] We first carry out horizontal stretches, followed by horizontal translations.
2. Then, we perform the transformations outside the argument of [MATH: f.] We first carry out vertical stretches, followed by vertical translations.

Content:
In this case, we begin by factoring out the coefficient next to the [MATH: x] inside the function:

Content:
[MATH: y = f\left(2x-4\right) +1 = f\left(2(x-2)\right) + 1]

Content:
Now, to plot [MATH: y=f\left(2(x-2)\right) +1,] we apply the following steps:

Content:
- Take the curve [MATH: y=f(x).]
- Stretch it by a scale factor of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}] parallel to the [MATH: x]-axis to get the graph of [MATH: y=f(2x).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/5da3ee21b747ff3a66334e943a80af53]

Content:
- Then, translate it to the right by [MATH: 2] units to get the graph of [MATH: y=f\left(2(x-2)\right).]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/edfabdc0ce3aa55003c5a89b2e58a0f2]

Content:
- There is no vertical scaling, so we omit this step.
- Finally, translate it up by [MATH: 1] unit to get the graph of [MATH: y=f\left(2(x-2)\right)+1.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d72618fd6b79e64857d9f0c6276696a3]

sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To perform transformations of functions with multiple operations, we must remember the following rule:

  1. First, we perform the transformations inside the argument of [MATH: f.] We first carry out horizontal stretches, followed by horizontal translations.

  2. Then, we perform the transformations outside the argument of [MATH: f.] We first carry out vertical stretches, followed by vertical translations.

First, let's factor out the coefficient next to the [MATH: x] inside the function:

[MATH: y = f\left(2x+2\right) -1 = f\left(2(x+1)\right) - 1]

To plot [MATH: y=f\left(2(x+1)\right) - 1,] we apply the following steps:

  • Take the curve [MATH: y=f(x).]

  • Stretch it by a scale factor of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}] parallel to the [MATH: x]-axis to get the graph of [MATH: y=f(2x).]

  • Then, translate it to the left by [MATH: 1] unit to get the graph of [MATH: y=f\left(2(x+1)\right).]

  • Finally, translate it down by [MATH: 1] unit to get the graph of [MATH: y=f\left(2(x+1)\right)-1.]

items.title: Determining the Correct Order of Transformations Given a Transformed Function Expression

sections.normalized_html:
The graph of [MATH: y=f\left(\dfrac x2-3\right)+5] can be obtained from the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] by applying some of the following transformations:

  • [MATH: (\textrm{T}1)] - Stretch by a scale factor of [MATH: 2] parallel to the [MATH: x]-axis

  • [MATH: (\textrm{T}2)] - Translate up by [MATH: 5] units

  • [MATH: (\textrm{T}3)] - Translate right by [MATH: 6] units

  • [MATH: (\textrm{T}4)] - Stretch by a scale factor of [MATH: \dfrac 12] parallel to the [MATH: x]-axis

What is a possible ordering of the appropriate transformations?

To get [MATH: y=f\left(\dfrac 12(x-6)\right)+5,] we could apply the following steps:

  • Apply transformation [MATH: (\textrm{T}1)\mathbin{:}] Stretch [MATH: y=f(x)] by a scale factor of [MATH: 2] parallel to the [MATH: x]-axis to get the graph of [MATH: y=f\left(\dfrac x2 \right).]

Therefore, a possible order of transformations is

[MATH: (\textrm{T}1) \to (\textrm{T}3) \to (\textrm{T}2).]

In this particular situation, we have to combine several operations.

Content:
To perform transformations of functions with multiple operations, we must apply the following rule:

Content:
1. First, we perform the transformations inside the argument of [MATH: f.] We first carry out horizontal stretches, followed by horizontal translations.
2. Then, we perform the transformations outside the argument of [MATH: f.] We first carry out vertical stretches, followed by vertical translations.

Item 8 — Example: Determining the Correct Order of Transformations Given a Transformed Function Expression

Example Prompt:
The graph of [MATH: y=f\left(\dfrac x2-3\right)+5] can be obtained from the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] by applying some of the following transformations:

- [MATH: (\textrm{T}1)] - Stretch by a scale factor of [MATH: 2] parallel to the [MATH: x]-axis
- [MATH: (\textrm{T}2)] - Translate up by [MATH: 5] units
- [MATH: (\textrm{T}3)] - Translate right by [MATH: 6] units
- [MATH: (\textrm{T}4)] - Stretch by a scale factor of [MATH: \dfrac 12] parallel to the [MATH: x]-axis

What is a possible ordering of the appropriate transformations?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To perform transformations of functions with multiple operations, we must remember the following rule:

1. First, we perform the transformations inside the argument of [MATH: f.] We first carry out horizontal stretches, followed by horizontal translations.
2. Then, we perform the transformations outside the argument of [MATH: f.] We first carry out vertical stretches, followed by vertical translations.

First, let's factor out the coefficient next to the [MATH: x] inside the function:

[MATH: y=f\left(\dfrac x2-3\right)+5 = f\left(\dfrac 12(x-6)\right)+5]

To get [MATH: y=f\left(\dfrac 12(x-6)\right)+5,] we could apply the following steps:

- Take the curve [MATH: y=f(x).]
- Apply transformation [MATH: (\textrm{T}1)\mathbin{:}] Stretch [MATH: y=f(x)] by a scale factor of [MATH: 2] parallel to the [MATH: x]-axis to get the graph of [MATH: y=f\left(\dfrac x2 \right).]
- Apply transformation [MATH: (\textrm{T}3)\mathbin{:}] Translate [MATH: y=f\left(\dfrac x2 \right)] right by [MATH: 6] units to get the graph of [MATH: y=f\left(\dfrac12{(x-6)}\right).]
- Apply transformation [MATH: (\textrm{T}2)\mathbin{:}] Translate [MATH: y=f\left(\dfrac12{(x-6)}\right)] up by [MATH: 5] units to get the graph of [MATH: y=f\left(\dfrac12{(x-6)}\right)+5.]

Therefore, a possible order of transformations is

[MATH: (\textrm{T}1) \to (\textrm{T}3) \to (\textrm{T}2).]
